outcome: Not settled, and no counterexample has been found: since 26 January 2024 the only dated items are two finite extensions of the computed range of primality in OEIS A005235 (first 4600 terms, 27 Aug 2026; first 5300 terms, 2 Oct 2026). Earlier, a 2023 journal article by Hayat Rezgui claims a proof 'in a particular case', which I could not read in full.
problem_asks: Let p_n# be the product of the first n primes and let a(n) be the least integer m > 1 such that p_n# + m is prime (the Fortunate numbers). The statement asks one thing: that every a(n), for every n >= 1, is prime; equivalently, that no Fortunate number is composite. Equivalent form: with q_n the least prime above p_n# + 1, q_n - p_n# is prime for all n. The statement places no restriction on n, so the quantity named is the universal claim over all n, and no sub-part of it is listed separately.

events.what_happened: S. W. Golomb, 'The evidence for Fortune's conjecture', Mathematics Magazine 54(4) (1981), pp. 209-210. Cited by OEIS A005235, the t5k glossary and MathWorld. I did not reach the text (the Taylor & Francis page was not opened). Per secondary citations it collects the numerical evidence available in 1981; the t5k glossary and OEIS say the conjecture first appeared in print in Gardner's Mathematical Games column in 1980.
events.delivers: Per secondary citations only: numerical and heuristic evidence for the conjecture; no proof is claimed in anything I could see.
events.direction: Evidence for the conjecture, no proof or counterexample claimed as far as the citations show.

events.what_happened: Charles R Greathouse IV, comment on OEIS A005235 (5 Jul 2011): 'The strong form of Cramér's conjecture implies that a(n) is a prime for n > 1618, as previously noted by Golomb.'
events.delivers: Conditional only: if the strong form of Cramér's conjecture holds, every Fortunate number with n > 1618 is prime. Nothing unconditional.
events.remains: The unconditional statement for all n, and every n <= 1618 even on the conditional route.
events.doubts: Rests on an open conjecture; Golomb's earlier remark was not located.
events.direction: Conditional support for the conjecture beyond n = 1618.
people: Solomon W. Golomb (earlier remark, as cited)

events.what_happened: Thomas Ordowski, comment on OEIS A005235 (9 Apr 2013): 'If a(n) < prime(n+1)^2 then a(n) is prime.' The reason is elementary: if a prime q <= p_n divided a(n), it would also divide p_n# and hence the prime p_n# + a(n), which is impossible since that number exceeds q. So every prime factor of a(n) exceeds p_n, and a composite a(n) is at least p_{n+1}^2.
events.delivers: Shows a(n) is prime whenever a(n) < p_{n+1}^2. Equivalently, a composite a(n) must be at least p_{n+1}^2. Covers only those n for which a(n) falls below that square; says nothing about n where it does not.
events.remains: Every n with a(n) >= p_{n+1}^2, which is the whole difficulty.
events.direction: Conditional criterion; supports the conjecture only under the bound a(n) < p_{n+1}^2.

events.what_happened: Joerg Arndt, comment on OEIS A005235 (15 Apr 2013): 'The first 2000 terms are primes.'
events.delivers: Finite computation: the first 2000 Fortunate numbers are prime. This moves no quantity the conjecture names, since it checks finitely many instances of a claim about all n.
events.directly_checkable: Each term is a primorial plus a least m; the check is a primality test on each term, reproducible from the OEIS programs.
events.doubts: The comment does not describe the computation.

events.what_happened: MathWorld's 'Fortunate Prime' entry states that values of F_k up to k = 100 are prime (attributed to Guy, 1994), 'a result extended to 1000 by E. W. Weisstein (Nov. 17, 2003)'.
events.delivers: Finite computation claimed: F_k prime for k <= 1000. This is a finite check and moves no quantity the conjecture names.
events.doubts: Reported second hand on MathWorld; the entry gives no method or program, and I did not inspect the computation.

events.what_happened: The Wikipedia article 'Fortunate number' states: 'As of 2017, all known Fortunate numbers are prime, checked up to n = 3000.' No source or method is given for the check. The article was last edited 24 August 2026, per the fetched page, and still lists the conjecture as unsolved.
events.delivers: A claimed finite check of primality to n = 3000 (primorial p_3000#). Unsourced. Moves no quantity the conjecture names.
events.doubts: Unsourced in the article. The OEIS table link attributes terms 2001-3000 to Pierre CAMI, whose comments on A005235 are dated 2017, which may be the source, but this is not stated and I have not confirmed it.

events.what_happened: Hayat Rezgui, 'Une preuve partielle de l'exactitude de la conjecture de Fortune, dans un cas particulier' (French; ResearchGate posting 365203314). According to the search tool's summary of the page, it was presented at a conference in Tamanghasset, Algeria, in November 2022, and its aim is to prove the conjecture in one particular case by studying intervals of a special form, using inequalities satisfied by fortunate numbers. The ResearchGate page returned HTTP 403 to my fetch, so I saw only the search summary.
events.revisions: Not established. It is probably an earlier form of the 2023 journal article (rezgui-2023-glm), which the journal received in July 2023. I did not check that they contain the same argument.
events.delivers: Per the search summary only: a proof of Fortune's conjecture in one particular case. The case is not described precisely in what I could read, so the restriction on n is unknown.
events.remains: The conjecture for all n outside that particular case, which the summary does not identify.
events.doubts: Preprint on ResearchGate, not a journal version. I found no commentary or citing work in my searches. The full text was not readable.
events.direction: Claims a proof in a restricted case. Cuts for the conjecture within that case only.
people: Hayat Rezgui (ENS Kouba, Algeria, per the search summary)

events.what_happened: Hayat Rezgui, 'An affirmative answer to Fortune's conjecture for all known fortunate numbers, with an optimal original inequality' (ResearchGate posting 366123299; dated 2022). According to the search summary, it aims to show that all known fortunate numbers satisfy a sharper inequality, and that if this inequality were extended to unknown fortunate numbers the conjecture would follow. The ResearchGate page returned HTTP 403 to my fetch.
events.delivers: Per the search summary: a check of a sharper inequality for the known fortunate numbers only, which is a finite set. The generalisation that would give the conjecture is stated as a conditional route, and the summary does not show that it was carried out.
events.remains: The conjecture for all n, and the extension of the inequality to unknown fortunate numbers.
events.doubts: The title claims an 'affirmative answer', but the summary describes a finite verification with a conditional extension. No peer review was found in my searches. Full text not readable.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture for known fortunate numbers; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Antonín Čejchan, Michal Křížek and Lawrence Somer, 'On Remarkable Properties of Primes Near Factorials and Primorials', Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), Article 22.1.4. From the HTML abstract page I opened: for the least prime p above n!+1, the claim that p - n! is prime is given a sufficient condition; there is an analogous statement for the largest prime below n!-1; and further sufficient conditions are given when n! is replaced by q#, the product of primes up to the prime q. The PDF returned binary and I could not read the theorems. OEIS A005235 cites this paper among its references.
events.revisions: Received 11 Nov 2021; revised version received 3 Jan 2022 (the page also lists 10 Jan 2022); published 10 Jan 2022. No arXiv version found. The date given is the journal publication, and an earlier public version may exist.
events.delivers: Sufficient conditions only. For the factorial case the abstract gives the range n!+1 < p < n!+r^2 (the HTML abstract prints it as n!+1 > p > n!+r^2; the search tool judged this a typo), with r the least prime above n. For the primorial analogue, if it has the same form, it covers the case a(n) < p_{n+1}^2, the same case as the 2013 OEIS criterion. Not verified from the PDF. It does not reach the conjecture for all n.
events.remains: The conjecture for every n with a(n) at or above the square of the next prime, which is every n outside the stated sufficient condition.

checked_by.who: Journal of Integer Sequences (refereed journal, hosted by the University of Waterloo)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the article after refereeing; I did not see the referee reports

events.doubts: The journal's own HTML page states the inequality for p in the opposite direction from the PDF, which the search tool judged a typo. I did not read the PDF theorems, so I cannot confirm the primorial statement.
events.direction: Sufficient condition only; supports the conjecture only within the stated bound.

events.what_happened: Hayat Rezgui, 'New explorations and remarkable inequalities related to Fortune's conjecture and fortunate numbers', General Letters in Mathematics 13(3) (1), pp. 58-76, DOI 10.31559/glm2023.13.3.1. I read the abstract on the journal page through the fetch tool, which returned key sentences rather than a verbatim abstract. Received 20/7/2023, revised 28/10/2023, accepted 4/11/2023, published 20/12/2023. The abstract's stated objectives are: 'Giving a proof of Fortune's conjecture in a particular case, by two different methods one of which is original'; 'Presenting many counterexamples ... when the satisfied hypothesis in that particular case, is not met'; and 'Proving a new remarkable inequality that all the 3000 first (known until now) fortunate numbers perfectly fulfill'.
events.revisions: Received 20/7/2023; revised 28/10/2023; accepted 4/11/2023. Two 2022 ResearchGate preprints by the same author carry the same subject (rezgui-2022-particular-case-preprint and rezgui-2022-affirmative-preprint). I could not check whether they contain the same argument. If they do, the first public written argument is from 2022, not the journal date; I have used the journal date because the 2022 texts were not readable.
events.delivers: Per the abstract: a proof of Fortune's conjecture for an unidentified particular case, by two methods; a new inequality checked on the first 3000 known fortunate numbers, which is a finite computation and moves no quantity the conjecture names. The particular case and its hypothesis are not stated in the abstract, and the theorem text was not readable. Restricted to that case.
events.remains: The conjecture for all n outside the particular case; the general conjecture as stated.
events.doubts: (1) The particular case and its hypothesis are not identified in anything I could read. (2) The refereeing standard of General Letters in Mathematics was not checked. (3) I found no commentary on the paper, and no later work I opened cites it: the Wikipedia article (fetched) and the OEIS A005235 reference list (fetched) do not. (4) The abstract's 'counterexamples' are cases where the particular case's hypothesis fails; the abstract itself says they do not disprove Fortune's conjecture.
events.direction: Claims a proof in a restricted case, cutting for the conjecture there. No counterexample to the conjecture is claimed.
events.object: No object exhibited against the conjecture. The 'counterexamples' in the abstract concern the case's hypothesis failing and are not described in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Hayat Rezgui, 'When Doesn't the Interval [a_{n+k}+P_n, a_{n+k+1}+P_n] Contain any Primes?', General Letters in Mathematics 12(4) (2022), pp. 164-168, DOI 10.31559/glm2022.12.4.2, where a_n is the nth prime and P_n is the nth prime factorial, per the search summary. The journal's topic list includes 'Fortune's conjecture'. I did not open this article.
events.delivers: Per the search summary only: such intervals contain no primes when a_{n+k+1} < a_{n+1}^2, with counterexamples when that inequality fails. It is about prime-free intervals, not directly about whether a(n) is prime. Whether the interval result feeds into Fortune's problem is not established.
events.remains: Fortune's question as stated, which the summary does not address.
events.doubts: I did not read the text. My reading that it does not bear on compositeness of a(n) is an inference from the summary and the journal's keyword list.
events.direction: A neighbouring result on prime-free intervals; says nothing stated about whether a(n) is prime.

events.what_happened: 'A Note on Large Prime Gaps' (Preprints.org manuscript 202408.1161) claims a disproof of Cramér's conjecture. Per the search summary, the page shows submitted 29 May 2025 and posted 4 June 2025, while the PDF footer carries a November 2024 date and a version 5 label, so the history is inconsistent. The page says it is not peer-reviewed. I did not open it.
events.revisions: Dates on the page and in the PDF footer conflict (PDF footer November 2024, version 5).
events.delivers: Claims a disproof of Cramér's conjecture. It concerns prime gaps. It bears on Fortune's problem only through the conditional route in greathouse-2011-oeis-conditional, whose hypothesis (the strong form of Cramér's conjecture) would then be false. That removes the conditional route and does not settle Fortune's conjecture either way.
events.doubts: Not peer-reviewed, per the page as summarised. I have not verified the argument.
events.direction: Neighbouring result; no direct bearing on whether a(n) is prime.

disputes.summary: OEIS A005235 cites 'Romeo Meštrović, arXiv:1202.3670, 2012' among its Fortunate-number references. The arXiv abstract page for 1202.3670 that I opened is 'Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes: a historical survey of its proofs (300 B.C.-2022) and another new proof' (v1 16 Feb 2012), which contains nothing about Fortunate numbers or Fortune's conjecture. Either the OEIS citation is wrong or the relevant material is in another version or paper I did not find.

summary: No source I could read reports that Fortune's conjecture has been settled, and none reports a counterexample. The record since the 26 January 2024 freeze is thin: two finite extensions of the checked range (first 4600 terms by Brock Falfas on 27 Aug 2026, first 5300 terms by Maik Pickl on 2 Oct 2026), both OEIS comments, which are finite checks that leave the universal claim untouched. The Wikipedia article, last edited 24 Aug 2026 per the fetch, still lists the conjecture as open and still cites only a 2017 check to n = 3000 with no source. The main pre-window work is a chain of finite checks (MathWorld's account of k <= 1000 in 2003, Arndt's 2000 terms in 2013, Wikipedia's unsourced n <= 3000 'as of 2017') and conditional or elementary criteria: Greathouse (2011) shows the strong form of Cramér's conjecture would give the statement for n > 1618, and Ordowski (2013) notes that a(n) < p_{n+1}^2 forces primality, because a composite a(n) must have all its prime factors above p_n and so be at least p_{n+1}^2. The one claimed partial proof is Hayat Rezgui's work: two 2022 ResearchGate preprints (one French, presented in Nov 2022 per the search summary; one English, which claims a finer inequality for known fortunate numbers), and the 2023 General Letters in Mathematics paper (published 20 Dec 2023), whose abstract claims a proof 'in a particular case' by two methods, plus a new inequality checked on the first 3000 known fortunate numbers. The abstract does not say which case; the PDF and the 2022 texts returned binary or HTTP 403, so I could not read the theorem. The Čejchan-Křížek-Somer paper (Journal of Integer Sequences, 10 Jan 2022) proves sufficient conditions for the factorial and primorial analogues, and OEIS cites it. Close reading: (a) the Rezgui 'particular case' may be the elementary criterion a(n) < p_{n+1}^2, which would make the 2023 claim a restatement of Ordowski's 2013 observation, with the 'remarkable inequality' perhaps the same bound checked for 3000 terms; (b) it may instead be a genuinely new restriction on n, which would be more than the criterion. I could not tell (a) from (b). No source names an AI system in connection with this problem (see ai fields). The AI search turned up only other problems: the OEIS Open benchmark (arXiv 2608.11941, 12 Aug 2026) names several systems and their results on OEIS conjectures, but its text has no hit for A005235 or 'Fortun', and the DeepMind formal-conjectures file for A005235 (FormalConjectures/OEIS/5235.lean) returned 404 on the main branch while the A080170 control file exists, so A005235 is probably not among the formalised OEIS conjectures in that repository. That is an inference from one repository, not a confirmed exclusion. The name 'Fortune' also collides with the Fortune magazine and with Reo Fortune's Fortunate numbers; the July 2026 Jacobian-conjecture counterexample credited to a Claude model and the May 2026 OpenAI unit-distance result concern other problems and are not events for this record.
competing_reading: Read the 2023 Rezgui article as a real, if partial, advance: it names a restricted class of n, proves the conjecture there by two methods, and reports an inequality on the first 3000 fortunate numbers that the author treats as new. Against that, the only elementary restricted case I can identify (a(n) < p_{n+1}^2) is known since 2013, and the 2022 Čejchan et al. paper proves its analogues. So the 'particular case' may be old, and the 2023 result may add a new name and a larger numerical check rather than a new restriction. Nothing I read decides between these readings.
what_would_settle_it: The full text of the 2023 General Letters in Mathematics article (or its 2022 ResearchGate preprints): the exact hypothesis of the 'particular case' and the statement of its theorem, and whether that hypothesis is a(n) < p_{n+1}^2 or something else. Also the PDF of Čejchan, Křížek and Somer (JIS 22.1.4): whether the primorial theorem is the same bound. A referee report or a citing paper engaging with either would count as human engagement. For the AI question, the OEIS Open GitHub release listing the 492 conjectures by A-number (to confirm whether A005235 is among them), and any authors' statement that a system was used on this sequence.

judgement.why: All post-snapshot items are finite checks (4600 and 5300 terms: instances) or a neighbouring prime-gap claim (variant). Conditional or sufficient-condition criteria (Greathouse, Ordowski, Čejchan-Křížek-Somer) do not settle any identifiable set of n unconditionally, so they are scored none rather than case: 'a(n) is prime whenever a(n) < p_{n+1}^2' is a reduction to an unproven condition on each n. Rezgui's 'particular case' claims are scored case but doubtful because the case is unidentified and may be that same criterion; all are pre-snapshot regardless. No AI involvement anywhere.
judgement.doubts: Rezgui 2023 and its 2022 preprint were not read in full; if their 'particular case' is just the a(n) < p_{n+1}^2 criterion, they should be none rather than case. This does not affect post-snapshot status.
